To find $\lim_{n \to \infty} d_n$, we note that $d_n = \frac{f^{(n)}(0)}{n!}$ is the coefficient of $x^n$ in the Maclaurin series expansion of $f(x)$.

The function is given by
$$
f(x) = \frac{(2025+x) \ln(2025+x)}{x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6} = \frac{(2025+x)\ln(2025+x)}{(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)}.
$$

The singularities of $f(x)$ in the complex plane are:
- Simple poles at the roots of the denominator: $x = 1$, $x = 2$, and $x = 3$.
- A branch point from the logarithm at $x = -2025$.

The singularity closest to the origin is the simple pole at $x = 1$. The asymptotic behavior of the Taylor coefficients $d_n$ as $n \to \infty$ is dominated by this nearest singularity. 

We can find the residue of $f(x)$ at $x = 1$:
$$
\operatorname{Res}(f, 1) = \lim_{x \to 1} (x - 1) f(x) = \frac{(2025+1) \ln(2025+1)}{(1 - 2)(1 - 3)} = \frac{2026 \ln(2026)}{(-1)(-2)} = 1013 \ln(2026).
$$

Near $x = 1$, the principal part of $f(x)$ is:
$$
\frac{\operatorname{Res}(f, 1)}{x - 1} = -\frac{1013 \ln(2026)}{1 - x} = -1013 \ln(2026) \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} x^n.
$$

Since all other singularities have modulus $|x| \ge 2$, their contributions to the $n^{\text{th}}$ coefficient are $O(2^{-n})$. Thus:
$$
d_n = -1013 \ln(2026) + O(2^{-n}).
$$

Taking the limit as $n \to \infty$:
$$
\lim_{n \to \infty} d_n = -1013 \ln(2026).
$$

ANSWER: -1013 \ln(2026)
